1380.bp: Enterprise software is filled with visual guides—screenshots, diagrams, video tutorials—that help people understand *how* to do things. When an employee asks a conversational AI system a question about a product, today it answers in plain text, missing all these images and videos that would actually show the answer clearly. This work tackles the real problem: how do we make AI assistants that pull up the right images and videos alongside text, turning vague answers into rich, visual instructions?
1380.wh: The hard part is that images and videos are not text. An image of a form or a flow diagram doesn't have obvious words to search by. You could write a caption or transcript, but captions often miss the most important visual details—the layout, the color coding, the spatial relationships that make something clickable or clear. Simply searching captions alone leaves relevant images unfound; yet you can't just match images to user questions directly without some connection through text.

The hard part is that images and videos are not text. An image of a form or a flow diagram doesn't have obvious words to search by. You could write a caption or transcript, but captions often miss the most important visual details—the layout, the color coding, the spatial relationships that make something clickable or clear. Simply searching captions alone leaves relevant images unfound; yet you can't just match images to user questions directly without some connection through text.
1380.ap: They use two search methods together. First, they search directly for images and videos by matching them (along with their captions) to the user's question. Second, they search for text passages in the documentation that match the question, then ask: what images and videos are linked to these text passages? By combining both results—direct visual matches and images attached to semantically related text—they recover images that caption-only search would miss. The final answer shows both text and the retrieved images side-by-side.
1380.ww: This works because images are rarely searched for in isolation; they live in a web of textual context. A screenshot might not have words describing its content, but the surrounding documentation text does. By finding text first, you locate the *context* where visual artifacts matter, then pull those artifacts forward. Direct visual search catches things captions describe well; text-based expansion catches things that live nearby but weren't captioned. Together, they cover both paths to finding an image.
1380.po: On real enterprise systems, this approach improves the ability to find the right images by 22% (measured as Hit@10—whether the correct image appears in the top 10 results) and improves recall by 20%. The payoff is concrete: when an employee asks how to do something, the system now surfaces actual screenshots and video clips that show the steps, not just a text explanation of them.

1381.bp: When a product team changes their ranking system and wants to know if the change is good, they run an A/B test: show the old system to some users, the new system to others, measure who makes more money. The problem is that revenue is lumpy—a handful of big spenders create almost all the money, while most users spend nothing. This lumpiness makes it hard to tell whether a small change actually helped, because luck and randomness drown out the signal.
1381.wh: Revenue metrics are dominated by outliers. Imagine 99 users spend a dollar, but 1 user spends a thousand; the mean revenue is $10.99, but it's entirely determined by one person. If that one person happens to see the new system, the test will look amazing even if the new system is worse. If they see the old system, it will look terrible. With such high variance, you need huge numbers of users to be confident in a result—which means running tests longer and slower.
1381.ap: They split users into groups based on their pre-experiment spending levels before the test even starts (a technique called post-stratification). They might group users into 'light spenders,' 'medium spenders,' and 'heavy spenders' based on historical data. Then within each group, they measure the effect separately and combine the results. This way, if a random whale lands in the new system, they account for it because they know what that whale's spending level usually is. They combine this grouping with another variance-reduction trick (CUPED), which uses historical spending patterns to smooth out noisy estimates.
1381.ww: The intuition is simple: variance comes from not knowing whether a big revenue difference is real or just unlucky user assignment. If you pre-split users by spending level, you control for that—you're comparing apples to apples within each tier. Heavy spenders will exist in both the test and control groups in predictable amounts, so their randomness washes out instead of creating false signals.
1381.po: The payoff is that the company can reach the same statistical confidence level using 45% fewer users. Instead of running a test for two weeks on a billion users, they might reach the same conclusion in one week on 500 million users. This is a direct business win: faster decisions, cheaper tests, ability to run more experiments.

1382.bp: On a platform like Pinterest, when you're looking at something you haven't seen before (a new pin, a fresh artist's work), the recommendation system struggles because it has no history of whether you like that creator's style. This is the cold-start problem: how do you recommend something *new* when you have no data points yet? The platform's business depends on helping creators get discovered and keeping users engaged, so getting cold-start right is crucial to long-term growth.
1382.wh: Normal recommendation systems learn from patterns: if you liked this 100 times, the system learns you like this kind of thing. But with a brand-new pin, there are no likes yet, no engagement signals. You can't learn from history that doesn't exist. You could use the content itself (the image, metadata) but that's noisy—many good pins get buried just because they haven't had time to rack up signals. You also have very little data about whether the creator's *previous* pins (if any) appeal to you, so you're flying blind on both fronts.
1382.ap: They use hierarchical item IDs learned from the dataset—think of this as a semantic taxonomy. Instead of just storing 'pin #4837291,' they store 'pin #4837291' as part of a tree: it's a 'fashion photo' → 'streetwear' → 'men's sneakers' → 'vintage-inspired.' This rich structure lets them make educated guesses about new pins by looking at semantic similarity before engagement data exists. They also add engagement information (how people interact with items) into the ID system itself, and use multiple view learning (comparing queries to items, items to each other) to align these representations with real engagement. On Pinterest's full system, they test this across multiple surfaces (Home Feed, Search, Closeup) and content types (organic pins, e-commerce products).
1382.ww: The core insight is that semantically similar things tend to get liked together. If the system understands that a new pin is 'mid-century modern furniture' (via the hierarchical ID), it can look at how users engaged with other mid-century pins and make a reasonable guess. The hierarchical structure also naturally helps with cold-start because fresh content shares semantic prefixes with established content, so the model generalizes knowledge. By encoding engagement patterns into the ID space itself, rather than treating IDs as opaque numbers, the system can predict engagement for truly new items.
1382.po: On Pinterest's production system serving billions of requests daily, this approach drives a 3.67% increase in fresh engagements (repins) and a 0.05% increase in daily active users retained, which at Pinterest's scale is enormous. The system has been deployed and is actively making recommendations at production scale.

1383.bp: Short-form video platforms like TikTok and Douyin live on two tensions: users want interesting content (so show what they'll watch), but creators need opportunities to grow their audience (so give emerging creators visibility). Right now, systems almost always choose: maximize watch time, even if it starves new creators. But if all creators give up, the platform dies. This paper asks: can we optimize *both* at once—make users happy *and* give creators a fair shot?
1383.wh: These two goals fight. The videos with the highest watch time tend to come from established creators with large audiences. If you always show those, users are happy but new creators get zero exposure. If you force exposure for new creators, users watch less and the platform's engagement tanks. Previous work either tackles one goal (maximize creator fairness) or ignores the creator side (just maximize views). The real challenge is that these aren't separate decisions you can optimize one by one—the system recommends videos to millions of users simultaneously, and those decisions ripple across the entire platform's creator economy.
1383.ap: They frame the problem as a constrained optimization: maximize total user satisfaction while ensuring creator exposure meets certain thresholds. The trick is that enforcing global constraints across all users in real time seems computationally impossible (checking millions of recommendations against a constraint is too slow). They use a primal-dual algorithm, which is a technique from optimization theory that decouples the global constraint into local decision rules. Each individual recommendation decision follows a simple rule derived from the global constraint, so you don't need to check all recommendations against each other—each one locally respects the global goal.
1383.ww: The insight is that global fairness doesn't require global coordination. By using primal-dual methods, they convert the problem from 'enforce a global constraint on millions of decisions' into 'apply a local rule to each individual decision.' The local rule is derived from the constraint mathematically, so following it automatically satisfies the global property. It's like saying instead of 'make sure exactly 5% of exposure goes to emerging creators,' you say 'each recommendation has a 5% chance of promoting an emerging creator,' and when you multiply that across millions of decisions, you hit the global target without any coordination.
1383.po: On a large-scale short-video platform, this approach achieves measurable improvements in joint user-creator value compared to baselines that optimize only one objective. The framework is practical enough to deploy in real systems where decisions must be made in milliseconds, suggesting the method unifies creator interests and user satisfaction without sacrificing platform speed.

1384.bp: In fashion and interior design, some combinations of items look great together and some clash—a sofa pairs well with certain tables but not others, a sweater matches some pants but not those. Recommending visually compatible items is a big part of e-commerce, from outfits to home decor. But 'compatible' is deeply contextual: mid-century modern furniture follows different rules than minimalist design; a navy sweater and a red scarf work together in ways a neon sweater and a bright red scarf might not. The goal is to teach machines to *see* these subtle visual rules.
1384.wh: Compatibility is not a property of individual items—it's a relationship between items in context. A generic image recognition system can tell you 'this is a brown sofa,' but it can't judge if that brown sofa matches a green chair without understanding style, material, period, and countless other nuances. Existing methods treat compatibility as a fixed property in some abstract space (like 'sofas go in this neighborhood, tables go in that one'), but that ignores the fact that a sofa's compatibility *depends* on which item you're pairing it with. A leather sofa pairs differently with a glass coffee table than with a rustic wood table.
1384.ap: They build a model that uses both images and text descriptions. The key idea is that compatibility is conditional—you're asking 'is this item compatible *with that item*?' They use an attention mechanism that looks at textual descriptions (like 'mid-century modern' or 'oak finish') to selectively focus on relevant visual features. Instead of learning one generic 'sofa representation,' the model learns to *highlight different parts* of the sofa image depending on what it's being paired with. When pairing a sofa with a table, emphasize wood tone and edge style; when pairing with a curtain, emphasize color and texture. They train this using triplets (compatible pairs and incompatible pairs) to learn these conditional compatibility rules.
1384.ww: The core insight is that vision and language collaborate on style. A visual model alone can't distinguish mid-century modern from minimalist without explicit guidance, but text ('mid-century modern') can. By conditioning visual attention on textual context, the model learns to weight visual features appropriately for each style. A text like 'oak finish' tells the model to pay attention to wood grain and color in the image, automatically making compatibility judgments that account for material. This is more flexible than rigid category-specific rules because new styles can be described in text without retraining.
1384.po: The model shows improvements on established fashion and interior design benchmarks. By leveraging text descriptions to guide visual understanding, the approach captures style nuances that image-only methods miss, enabling more accurate recommendations of visually compatible items—tangibly useful for e-commerce platforms trying to help customers find items that work together.

1385.bp: E-commerce marketplaces like Amazon and local classified platforms operate under countless rules: no counterfeit items, no misleading photos, no prohibited substances. When someone lists a product, that listing must be checked against every rule to ensure it's allowed. With millions of daily submissions and thousands of rules, checking every listing against every policy is computationally prohibitive. The goal is to quickly filter safe items and flag suspicious ones for human review, without checking everything exhaustively.
1385.wh: The naive approach—test each new listing against each of the thousand policies—is too slow. It would create a bottleneck that slows down the marketplace's ability to accept new listings. You need a fast filter that catches problematic items before they reach the expensive verification step. But the filter must have high recall: missing a policy violation is worse than being a bit overzealous and flagging something for further review. So you need speed *and* accuracy, which don't usually go together.
1385.ap: They use language models to convert policy documents (which are often complex legal text) into concise, searchable descriptions. These descriptions are stored in a vector index (a searchable space where similar items live nearby). When a new product is listed, they quickly search this index to find which policies are most likely relevant to that item. This acts as a high-speed router: most items get a quick 'looks fine' result and skip the expensive verification step, while suspicious items are routed to specific policy classes for deeper checking. To improve accuracy, they use hard negative samples—when training, they deliberately feed the model examples of items that *almost* violate a policy but don't quite, forcing it to learn the boundaries more precisely.
1385.ww: The efficiency comes from search instead of exhaustive testing. Instead of running a complex rule engine on every item for every policy, you ask: which policies are *relevant* to this item? Then you only check the relevant ones. Using language models to compress policies into searchable vectors makes this possible. Hard negatives improve accuracy because they teach the model that being 'close to' a violation is still different from violating—an item that almost looks counterfeit but isn't is valuable training data for understanding where the line is.
1385.po: On an internal e-commerce dataset, this retrieval-based approach achieves 3.8% better recall at a fixed rate of false positives compared to standard dense retrieval. Adding hard negative examples to the index improves recall by 26.3% on average. The practical payoff is that the system can filter listings much faster without needing to manually check every listing against every rule.

1386.bp: Large language models like GPT can answer questions about business data—'what revenue did we get from sales in July?'—by reading a CSV or database table and synthesizing an answer. But hallucination is a killer risk: if the model makes up a number or misinterprets the data, a business decision based on that answer could be wrong. This work tackles the specific problem of making table question answering reliable enough for production analytics, where a wrong answer costs money or credibility.
1386.wh: Direct preference optimization (a popular technique for making language models better at following instructions) works by showing the model pairs of answers: 'this is a good answer, this is a bad answer.' But it doesn't capture *why* one is better. Maybe one answer is more accurate, another more helpful. By mixing these signals, the model learns a blurry notion of 'good.' For table question answering, you need the model to deeply understand *factual correctness*, not just general helpfulness. The existing approach throws away the reason behind each preference, losing information.
1386.ap: They introduce a reason-aware version of preference optimization. Instead of just showing 'answer A is better than answer B,' they show 'answer A is better than answer B *because* [reason: it correctly joins the tables / interprets the date filter / aggregates the right column].' The model learns these explicit reasons alongside the preference, so it learns to internalize what makes a factually accurate answer. The reasons act as a bridge that helps the model understand *why* a table query is right or wrong, not just that one answer is preferred.
1386.ww: Reasons act as an explanation layer that makes learning more precise. When a model learns from a reason ('the answer is wrong because it summed the wrong column'), it can't just learn a superficial preference—it must reason about the structure of the problem. Over time, it internalizes these reasoning patterns, making it better at handling new queries. The reason essentially decomposes a complex preference signal into interpretable steps, which helps the model generalize to cases it hasn't seen.
1386.po: Evaluated on real-world advertising datasets, RAPO shows substantial improvements over standard preference optimization in factual accuracy. The payoff is that language models become more trustworthy for answering business-critical questions over structured data, reducing hallucination risk in production analytics.

1387.bp: Customer service AI systems often recommend actions to customers: 'Click here to reset your password,' 'Follow these steps to change your shipping address.' The system's job is to guess what the user actually needs right now. It currently looks at the customer's past interactions ('they reset their password last month, so they probably need account help') but ignores a key insight: what a customer *needs now* is connected to what they're *about to do next*. If they're about to leave a product review, they might need formatting help; if they're about to make a purchase, they might need payment options. The goal is to make these intent recommendations more accurate by predicting the next action.
1387.wh: Historical behavior alone is a lagging indicator. By the time a customer clicks 'reset password,' they've already decided they need to reset. The system's recommendation comes too late or is already obvious. More subtly, what the customer needs depends on their trajectory—where they're going next—not just where they've been. A customer who looked at product pages and then went to checkout needs different help than a customer who looked at product pages and then left. Current methods ignore this forward-looking signal.
1387.ap: They build a model that first predicts what the customer will do next (next action/behavior). This prediction happens in two ways: (1) forward deduction—looking at past actions and inferring likely continuations, and (2) reverse tracing—working backward from known action sequences to fill in gaps. They supervise this with 'closed-loop' feedback: comparing predicted next actions to what actually happened later. Then they use this predicted-next-action to guide the main intent recommendation model, progressively activating latent representations in the model that correspond to the anticipated next action.
1387.ww: The insight is that next actions and current intent are coupled. If you accurately predict what someone will do next, you can align your current recommendation to match. When you predict 'this customer is about to review a product,' you can recommend 'here's how to write a review' rather than generic help. The closed-loop training ensures the next-action predictor is calibrated to real behavior, not just theoretically plausible—so it's actually useful for guiding the main model.
1387.po: On offline experiments, the model shows effectiveness in capturing intent. In online A/B testing on a real customer service platform, NBA-Net achieves a 5.6% relative improvement in click-through rate, meaning more customers use the recommended actions. This is a concrete gain in system usefulness.

1388.bp: In emerging-market e-commerce, platforms often have basic product categories ('clothing,' 'electronics') but lack detailed attributes ('material: cotton,' 'brand: Nike,' 'size: M'). Without these fine-grained attributes, search is weak—customers can't filter 'show me blue cotton shirts' because the system doesn't know material or color. Rebuilding this from scratch by hand is expensive and slow. This work automates bootstrapping of product attribute taxonomies using language models and human feedback, starting from absolutely nothing.
1388.wh: Creating an attribute taxonomy is hard because you need to: (1) figure out what attributes even matter (different product categories need different attributes), (2) define the valid values for each attribute (colors, sizes, materials), (3) validate that the taxonomy actually works for the product catalog. A language model might generate plausible attributes, but they could be wrong, redundant, or miss domain nuances. You need human validation, but that's expensive. Existing solutions either require hand-labeling (slow, expensive) or use generic attribute ontologies that don't fit emerging markets.
1388.ap: They use a human-in-the-loop pipeline. A language model generates candidate attributes for a product category. Then two stages of human review: (1) developers spot-check for nonsense and filter out bad suggestions before they go to the second stage, and (2) local domain-expert staff validate and refine the attributes. This feedback is fed back into the generation pipeline—each round, the prompts are tweaked based on what went wrong before. The loop repeats until the taxonomy stabilizes. Once the taxonomy is solid, language models tag individual products with their attributes, enriching the catalog.
1388.ww: Human-in-the-loop works here because the loop is tight and local. Each iteration, humans see concrete outputs ('the model suggested 'color' is an attribute, is that right?') and can give targeted feedback. Developer review catches obvious errors quickly, so domain experts aren't wasting time on garbage; expert validation catches domain-specific nuances that models miss. By cycling feedback directly back into prompts, the language model learns to align with local expectations.
1388.po: Once the attribute taxonomy is built, the platform gains multiple benefits: customers can now do faceted filtering ('show me blue cotton shirts only'), ranking models get structured features to learn from, and dense retrieval (semantic search) gets richer representations to work with. The real payoff is that platforms in emerging markets can now bootstrap sophisticated search without enormous upfront tagging effort.

1389.bp: Fashion e-commerce platforms use vision-language models (AI systems that understand both images and text) to extract structured information from product photos: 'what brand is this?' 'what color?' 'what material?' But these models are general-purpose (trained on internet images) and haven't been tuned for fashion. Before betting on a model for production, teams need to know: which model actually works best for our specific tasks? How sensitive is each model to how you ask it questions? This work creates a benchmark to answer these questions in real e-commerce settings.
1389.wh: Off-the-shelf vision-language models weren't designed for fashion extraction. A model trained to caption generic internet images might struggle with fashion-specific attributes or the structured extraction tasks that e-commerce workflows demand. Testing every model on every task is expensive and slow. Moreover, different models behave differently depending on the prompt (how you phrase the question), and some models update over time, sometimes improving and sometimes degrading. You need a benchmark that captures these production realities.
1389.ap: They define five specific extraction tasks across two types of images (outfit photos and individual product photos) and test six commercial and two open-source models with multiple prompt variants. They try a standard prompt and model-specific prompts (prompts the model's creators suggested as optimal). For each model-prompt-task combination, they measure success and analyze error patterns. The benchmark is grounded in real fashion e-commerce needs, not generic vision tasks.
1389.ww: Benchmarking reveals task-specific patterns. The finding that best-performing models vary by task means no single model is universally best—you must evaluate on *your* tasks. Error patterns being model-dependent rather than prompt-dependent means you can't fix a bad model just by asking better; the model itself matters. Updates sometimes helping and sometimes hurting specific tasks shows that model versions aren't uniformly better, so you need continuous monitoring.
1389.po: The benchmark provides concrete guidance for teams deploying vision-language models in fashion: evaluate on your specific tasks, don't trust generic benchmarks, and monitor continuously as models update. This is a practical contribution—it doesn't build a better model, but it shows teams how to rigorously evaluate candidates before production deployment.

1390.bp: Search and recommendation systems rank results by relevance, but e-commerce platforms also want to make money. They can rerank the top results to promote 'sponsored' (paid) listings, or products with higher profit margins, increasing platform revenue. But reranking too aggressively kills relevance—if users don't find what they searched for, they'll shop elsewhere. The problem is balancing revenue against relevance and fraud constraints: maximize money without tanking user satisfaction or promoting scams.
1390.wh: The naive approach—just promote sponsored items to the top—destroys relevance and user trust. A principled approach would solve a mathematical optimization problem: 'maximize revenue subject to keeping relevance above a threshold and fraud risk below a threshold.' But solving this perfectly for every single search query is computationally expensive; you need an answer in milliseconds for a live search. Exact optimization is too slow for production.
1390.ap: They formulate the problem as an integer linear program (a mathematical optimization problem) and then build a lightweight approximation algorithm called PermR (permutation reranking). PermR works by repeatedly looking at adjacent pairs of results in the ranking and deciding whether to swap them. Each swap either improves revenue or fixes a violated constraint (brings fraud risk under control, or pushes relevance back above the threshold). The algorithm terminates when no swaps improve things further. This greedy approach is fast enough to run per-query at production latency.
1390.ww: The approximation works because you don't need the mathematically perfect answer—you need a good-enough answer fast. Swapping adjacent items is a simple local operation: if reranking item 5 and 6 helps, do it; repeat. This greedy strategy doesn't find the global optimum, but it finds a reasonable solution quickly. The constraints (keep relevance above X, keep fraud below Y) are maintained throughout, so you never accidentally create a bad ranking just to squeeze out one more dollar.
1390.po: In offline testing across multiple e-commerce categories, PermR achieves about 63% of the ideal revenue improvement that perfect optimization would provide, while staying within production latency limits and respecting all constraints. In a 14-day online A/B test on 56 million search queries, PermR increased platform revenue by 2%, demonstrating the approach works at scale.

1391.bp: Short-form video platforms like TikTok serve recommendations based on watching history. A user might have watched hundreds or thousands of videos, and the system needs to learn their patterns from all of that. The longer the history you use, the better you might understand them—but processing thousands of items is computationally expensive. Modern deep learning systems (Transformers) get slower as sequences get longer because they compare every item to every other item. The goal is to handle ultra-long watch histories at billion-user scale while staying within computational budgets.
1391.wh: There are two bottlenecks. First, video IDs are typically just numbers ('video #482916') which don't carry meaning—the system has to learn what that ID means by looking it up in a table. As the catalog grows to billions of videos, the lookup table gets huge, and cold-start (recommending new videos) is hard because the ID has no semantic signal. Second, Transformers scale poorly: comparing every item to every other item takes quadratic time, so increasing watch history from 100 to 1000 items doesn't just take 10x longer, it takes 100x longer. For a billion-user platform, this becomes prohibitive.
1391.ap: They replace raw video IDs with semantic IDs—a hierarchical structure where each ID encodes content type, genre, and specifics. Instead of just 'video #482916,' it's 'short-form video → comedy → sketch comedy → group jokes.' This hierarchical structure is much smaller than listing every possible video individually. For the computational problem, they build a new Transformer layer that compresses long sequences using temporal folding (grouping nearby items) and global query integration (summarizing key information globally). These techniques reduce the quadratic complexity of standard attention to something more manageable.
1391.ww: Semantic IDs reduce the problem's size. By using hierarchy, you shrink embedding tables from billions of entries to thousands of semantic nodes, and new videos automatically share the semantic prefixes of similar content (solving cold-start). Temporal folding works because watch patterns often have local structure—consecutive videos watched in a session probably reflect immediate interests—so you can combine nearby items without losing much information. Global queries ensure rare but important information isn't lost in the compression.
1391.po: On production infrastructure, this framework reduces peak memory usage by an order of magnitude and dramatically reduces computation time, allowing the system to model ultra-long sequences at billion-scale. The semantic IDs also help with cold-start, since new videos inherit meaning from their semantic ancestors. This enables the platform to personalize recommendations based on vastly longer watch histories than previously possible.

1392.bp: Large-scale recommendation systems at companies like Alibaba use a two-tower architecture for speed: one tower learns user representations, another learns item representations. They compare them quickly at recommendation time. This architecture is fast, but the downside is that the two towers are independent, so the system can't easily use fine-grained information about how this specific user might interact with this specific item (what fashion researchers call 'interaction effects'). The goal is to inject more semantic understanding into pre-ranking—the fast first stage of ranking—without sacrificing the speed advantage.
1392.wh: Two-tower models are decoupled for efficiency—each tower can be computed independently and in parallel. But this decoupling is also their weakness: they can't see the target item during user representation, so they can't capture subtle user-item interactions. A user might like minimalist fashion in general, but hate minimalist shoes; standard two-tower models would struggle with these fine-grained preferences because they learn a single 'user representation' that doesn't know which item it's being matched against.
1392.ap: PGSF is a plug-in that works during training but preserves the two-tower efficiency at serving time. During training, they (1) use the target item to guide user representation learning, creating item-aware user profiles, (2) build a discrete semantic space of user interests (using RQ-VAE, a compression technique), and (3) hierarchically select interests from that space relevant to the target item. At serving time, the two towers remain decoupled and fast—the system only uses the pre-computed user and item representations. The training procedure learns to bake item-awareness into the representations without requiring item information at serving time.
1392.ww: The trick is that information baked into a representation at training time is still there at serving time, even if you stop providing the information. By training the user tower with knowledge of the target item, the learned user representation implicitly captures patterns about which items matter for which users. When you serve only the representation (not the items), that knowledge is latent but present. This lets you get some of the accuracy benefits of joint user-item modeling while keeping the speed of decoupled inference.
1392.po: On Tmall App (Alibaba's shopping platform), PGSF shows +2.66% improvement in clicked-through items and +3.13% improvement in page views. The system integrates smoothly into existing two-tower setups, meaning it can be deployed without overhauling existing infrastructure. Code is published, suggesting it's a practical technique other platforms can adopt.

1393.bp: Novelty is the enemy of boredom. If a recommendation system only shows users what they already like, they'll watch the same content forever and eventually get bored. But novelty must be *relevant*—showing completely random content isn't novelty, it's annoyance. This work tackles the hard problem: how do you compose recommendation lists that are both personally relevant *and* meaningfully different from what the user has recently consumed, on a platform with millions of users and hundreds of thousands of items?
1393.wh: Maximizing relevance and maximizing novelty are in tension. The most relevant item is probably similar to things the user watched yesterday. The most novel item is probably something they'd hate. Prior work either optimizes relevance alone (boring lists), or adds a diversity penalty without really understanding how to balance the two. Language models offer a new angle—they can reason through both objectives, but they need supervision to do it well. However, supervision is scarce: you can't ask humans to label 'is this list the right balance of relevant and diverse?'
1393.ap: BALANCE decomposes novelty recommendation into three stages that an LLM reasons through step-by-step. First, generate a 'Novelty Tag' that specifies an exploration direction ('I've watched a lot of cooking content, explore food from other cultures'). Second, refine an 'Interest Topic' that specifies the user's intent in concrete terms ('recipe discovery for international cuisines'). Third, construct the actual recommendation list ensuring facet coverage (diverse types of international recipes). To handle data scarcity, they synthesize training data by mixing real behavior logs with structured explanations of novelty transitions. To fix a reward mismatch (standard reinforcement learning gives one reward per list, but item-level errors matter), they use a new optimization method (SIPO) that balances both list-level and item-level rewards.
1393.ww: Breaking the problem into three stages makes it learnable. Each stage has clear semantics (novelty direction, interest topic, facet coverage), so the model can reason through them. Synthesized supervision gets around the scarcity problem by using real behavior to ground the reasoning—if someone switched from cooking to food travel content, that's a real novelty transition; the model learns from that. Joint sequence-and-item rewards matter because one item-level error (recommending something totally irrelevant) ruins the whole list; by optimizing both granularities, the model learns to construct cohesive, diverse lists.
1393.po: On a large e-commerce platform, this hierarchical reasoning framework improves novelty recommendation over baselines that optimize either relevance alone or relevance with a simple diversity penalty. The approach enables the platform to surface content that keeps users engaged over the long term by introducing meaningful variety, not just optimizing one-day relevance.

1394.bp: On e-commerce platforms, when you buy something, you might use a discount code or it might be on sale. The platform wants to predict whether you'll complete the purchase (conversion rate). They use this prediction to rank products in search results or recommend them. But most models ignore a key signal: the discount rate. If an item is 50% off, you're much more likely to buy. If the price is marked up 200%, you'll walk away. The goal is to build a model that understands how discounts drive purchasing decisions.
1394.wh: Discount rates are important for conversion but tricky to model. Discount patterns are complex: some users respond strongly to discounts (discount hunters), others ignore them (brand loyalists); seasonal promotions have periodic patterns (higher discounts during holidays); and discounts correlate with user spending habits (big spenders might not care about a 10% off sale). Models that ignore discounts miss this signal. Models that naively add discount as a feature often learn spurious patterns because discounts are non-uniformly distributed—heavy discounts on clearance items, zero discounts on premium items—creating confounding.
1394.ap: They build DANet (Discount-Aware Network) with three specialized components: (1) a time-frequency module that transforms discount history using Fourier analysis to capture long-term trends and periodic patterns (seasonal effects), (2) a distribution de-bias module that removes confounding from user-specific and promotion-specific discount patterns, and (3) a supervised auxiliary task that predicts the item's discount level, forcing the model to learn explicit discount representations. The auxiliary task acts as a regularizer: by making the model predict discount amount directly, it ensures discount information is properly learned rather than ignored.
1394.ww: Frequency analysis (Fourier transform) captures patterns across time. A discount pattern that repeats every month will show up as a peak in the frequency spectrum, letting the model distinguish periodic promotions from random discounts. De-biasing works because it separates real signals from confounding: a user might buy more when there's a discount, but that's partly because deep-discount items are already more likely to be bought. By separating the discount effect from the item-effect, the model learns the true conversion lift from discounts. The auxiliary task works because predicting discount level is an easier subgoal that forces the model to encode discount information before predicting conversion.
1394.po: On real e-commerce datasets, DANet improves offline AUC (a standard ranking metric) by 1.61%, and online A/B testing shows 3.63% improvement in conversion rate (pCVR) and 2.23% improvement in gross merchandise value (GMV). The approach has been deployed successfully on e-commerce platforms, meaning it's production-ready and delivers measurable business value.
